title: MFA tiers: SMS, TOTP, hardware keys
body_md:
## Choose MFA for the attack it must stop

MFA asks for more than a password, but methods differ in what they stop. The useful question is not “do I have two steps?” It is “can an attacker who knows my password, controls my phone number, or operates a fake login still get in?” Use the strongest method your real service and recovery plan support; leaving an account with no MFA while waiting for a perfect option is usually worse.

### The methods and their limits

**SMS or voice codes** add a barrier against simple password reuse. A number can be reassigned or hijacked by a SIM swap, and a code can be talked out of you or entered into a fake login. If SMS is the only offered option, it is often better than none; ask your carrier about account PIN or number-transfer protection, where offered.

**Authenticator-app codes (TOTP)** come from a shared secret enrolled with a service. The app may store or sync that seed depending on its settings, so “only on this phone” is not a universal property. TOTP avoids SMS-number takeover, but the code is still manually entered and can be relayed by a phishing site in real time. Store recovery codes securely and understand how to move to a replacement device before discarding the old one.

**FIDO security keys and passkeys** use cryptographic credentials bound to the real service's domain. Properly implemented WebAuthn authentication prevents a lookalike site from obtaining a valid response for the target service. A physical key is generally bound to that device; a passkey can be synced or device-bound, depending on its provider. Both still depend on service configuration, a secure device, and recovery choices. A site might keep SMS as an alternate route even after you register a key. Review the complete sign-in and recovery settings rather than assuming the strongest enrolled factor is the only path.

Email, password manager and any account that resets others deserve early attention. Financial and work accounts may offer only a subset; use their strongest available option, ask the institution about alternatives, and do not bypass workplace policy. If a code arrives unexpectedly, do not approve or share it. Open the service independently and inspect recent activity. Never give a code to a person who called you, even if they claim to be support.

widget_config.goal: Select and configure an MFA method by its phishing and recovery limits, not by a simple ranking label.
widget_config.today_action: Inspect MFA and recovery on your primary email; enable the strongest supported method you can back up, save recovery codes safely, and note any weaker alternate sign-in routes.
widget_config.scope: General comparison; actual options vary by service, carrier and jurisdiction. NIST is a US federal technical standard. Checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: A live code request during a fake login
blocks.situation: A synthetic “support agent” calls while you are on a login page and asks you to read a new app code to cancel an attempted sign-in.
blocks.analysis: The code could complete an attacker’s live login; TOTP and SMS are not phishing-resistant. End the call, open the official service independently, and inspect activity. Never read the code to the caller.

blocks.title: A bank offers only SMS
blocks.situation: A synthetic bank account has password plus SMS verification and no app, key or passkey option in its published settings.
blocks.analysis: SMS still adds a barrier compared with password alone. Keep it, secure the carrier account if available, and ask the bank about stronger options. Do not disable the only second step merely because it is weaker than a key.

blocks.title: Harden a travel-critical mailbox
blocks.setup: Four independent snapshots of synthetic travel-critical mailboxes. Each prompt supplies its own starting facts; an earlier choice does not change a later snapshot.

steps.prompt: Snapshot 1: A travel-critical mailbox offers SMS, authenticator codes and FIDO keys. You are signed in on its verified security page, with no key enrolled yet. Which factor will you enroll first for phishing resistance?

choices.text: Keep only SMS because it is the easiest second step.
choices.consequence: Password theft is harder to exploit, but SIM takeover and code relay remain.
choices.explanation: SMS is useful when needed, but a stronger available factor addresses more threats.

choices.text: Register a FIDO key on the mailbox’s verified security page.
choices.consequence: A properly configured WebAuthn login is bound to the service domain.
choices.explanation: Manual codes can be relayed; WebAuthn protects this authentication step.

steps.prompt: Snapshot 2: A mailbox already has one FIDO key enrolled, and you have a spare key. The service offers a second key slot and recovery codes. How do you prepare for loss of the first key?

choices.text: Register the spare key and store recovery codes separately in a protected place.
choices.consequence: Loss of the daily key need not mean account loss.
choices.explanation: Recovery must be planned while you still have access; protect backup routes.

choices.text: Skip backups because FIDO can never fail.
choices.consequence: Losing or damaging the only key could lock you out.
choices.explanation: Phishing resistance does not solve loss of the authenticator.

steps.prompt: Snapshot 3: A mailbox has a FIDO key enrolled, but SMS remains enabled as an alternate sign-in route. What does that mean?

choices.text: Review whether it can be removed safely or is needed for recovery; document the residual risk.
choices.consequence: You understand the actual weakest supported route.
choices.explanation: Enrolling a key does not automatically retire every fallback.

choices.text: The key makes all remaining routes phishing-resistant.
choices.consequence: A weaker fallback may still work.
choices.explanation: Security depends on all available sign-in and recovery paths.

steps.prompt: Snapshot 4: MFA is active on a mailbox. An unsolicited sign-in code arrives. What do you do?

choices.text: Read it to the caller claiming to be support.
choices.consequence: The caller may finish a login.
choices.explanation: Real support should not need your one-time sign-in code.

choices.text: Do not share or approve it; open the mailbox independently and review activity.
choices.consequence: No attacker receives the one-time credential.
choices.explanation: An unexpected code can mean a mistake or an attempted login; verify without using the message link.

blocks.debrief: These are four independent MFA decisions. For each account, pair the strongest available factor with a usable backup and review every fallback route. Retry a missed decision before mapping the pattern to a real account.

questions.prompt: What threat does TOTP remove relative to SMS?

choices.text: Dependence on control of the mobile number for generating the code.
choices.explanation: An app-generated code does not require delivery to the phone number.

choices.text: All phishing in which a fake page asks for a code.
choices.explanation: A manually entered TOTP code can be relayed.

questions.prompt: A site supports only SMS MFA. What is a practical choice?

choices.text: Use no MFA until hardware keys become available.
choices.explanation: That leaves the account exposed to password-only login.

choices.text: Enable it, protect the carrier account where possible, and monitor for stronger options.
choices.explanation: A weaker available factor can still reduce password-only risk.

questions.prompt: What property makes correctly configured FIDO login phishing-resistant?

choices.text: The key sends a longer code that is harder to type.
choices.explanation: The protection is cryptographic binding, not code length.

choices.text: The authentication response is bound to the real service identifier.
choices.explanation: A lookalike origin cannot reuse a valid response for the target.
